questions.question: Why should the Node.js version in a GitHub Actions workflow come from config instead of being hardcoded?
choices: Hardcoded values are faster to execute
Different projects use different Node versions, and hardcoded values break when the project upgrades
GitHub Actions rejects hardcoded version strings
It doesn't matter — all Node versions are backward compatible
questions.explanation: A hardcoded node-version: '18' will fail if the project upgrades to Node 20. Configurable versions let the workflow adapt to the project's actual requirements without editing the YAML.

questions.question: In a standard CI pipeline, what is the correct order of steps?
choices: Checkout → Setup Node → Install → Lint → Test → Build
questions.explanation: You must checkout the code first, then set up the runtime, install dependencies, and only then can you lint, test, and build. Running tests before install will always fail.

questions.question: What happens if a GitHub Actions workflow is missing the checkout step?
choices: The workflow runs on a blank environment with no code
GitHub automatically checks out the default branch
The workflow fails immediately with an error
The build step uses cached code from previous runs
questions.explanation: Without actions/checkout@v4, the runner has no source code. Subsequent steps like npm install or npm test will fail because there's no package.json or source files to work with.
